prompt:
You are a junior associate in the litigation group at Wexford Strait & Akiyama LLP. Supervising partner Alex Carbonneau has assigned you a motion to dismiss for breach of contract on behalf of Meridian Logistics, LLC. A copy of the relevant excerpt from the complaint and supporting exhibits is attached.

Your task is to prepare a motion to dismiss under CPLR 3211(a), together with a supporting memorandum of law, arguing all viable grounds for dismissal of the plaintiff's breach-of-contract claim. The motion should be framed from the defendant's perspective and formatted following standard New York state court motion practice conventions, including a proper caption, signature block, and firm header consistent with our internal templates.

The memorandum of law should include a statement of facts, argument sections with clear headings, and a conclusion. You need to identify every colorable basis for dismissal under CPLR 3211(a) as applied to a breach-of-contract cause of action and develop each argument with sufficient analysis.

Carbonneau has flagged the recent Court of Appeals decision in *Matter of New York Civil Liberties Union v. City of Rochester*, 2025 NY Slip Op 01010 (Feb. 20, 2025), as potentially relevant. That case concerns FOIL and the public disclosure of law enforcement disciplinary records following the 2020 repeal of Civil Rights Law § 50-a. Where you can draw a useful analogy to support dismissal — particularly on any argument touching contractual obligations around disclosure or information handling — cite it. Where its applicability to a breach-of-contract context is tenuous, distinguish it and note the weakness so the partner can assess litigation risk before filing. Remember to include the statutory notice per Judiciary Law § 431 that the opinion is uncorrected and subject to revision.

Use Bluebook citation format throughout. If the memorandum exceeds ten pages, include a table of contents and table of authorities. The final deliverable should be submitted as a single PDF.

sections.heading: Introduction
required_content: Context and purpose of the document
paragraphs: **INTRODUCTION**

This memorandum of law is submitted on behalf of the Petitioner in connection with the above-captioned Article 78 proceeding. The purpose of this document is to establish the legal and factual foundation for the Petitioner’s challenge to the final determination of the [Name of Respondent Agency/Administrative Body] (hereinafter “the Agency”), which denied the Petitioner’s application for [State specific permit, license, or approval, e.g., “a conditional use permit”] and imposed an unlawful condition upon its [related, distinct property right or activity]. The Agency’s determination was arbitrary and capricious, an abuse of discretion, and affected by an error of law, warranting its annulment by this Court.

The proceeding is governed by the standards for judicial review of administrative determinations as set forth in Article 78 of the Civil Practice Law and Rules and the applicable principles of substantive due process. In reviewing an agency’s decision, this Court is limited to ascertaining whether the determination has a rational basis and is supported by substantial evidence, or whether it is so lacking in reason that it constitutes an abuse of discretion. As the Court of Appeals has articulated, an administrative agency’s interpretation of the statutes and regulations it is charged with implementing is entitled to deference, provided that the interpretation is not irrational or unreasonable. This principle was expressly reaffirmed in *Matter of New York Civ. Liberties Union v. City of Rochester* (2025 NY Slip Op 01010), where the Court scrutinized the City’s statutory interpretation to ensure it was consistent with the legislative text and purpose, demonstrating that judicial deference has definable limits when an agency’s reading contravenes clear statutory language or results in an outcome incompatible with the governing law’s fundamental objectives.

The Petitioner will demonstrate that the Agency’s decision lacks a rational basis in fact and law. The record before the Agency was devoid of substantial evidence to support the specific finding upon which the denial or condition was predicated. Furthermore, the Agency’s action contravenes the explicit requirements of [cite relevant State statute, e.g., “Municipal Home Rule Law § 10”] and the [Name of Town/City] Zoning Code, § [Relevant Section], which establish clear criteria for the approval at issue. The Agency improperly relied upon considerations outside its statutory authority, thereby acting beyond the scope of its delegated powers and undermining the predictable and consistent application of local land use laws.

Consequently, this memorandum will argue that the Agency’s determination must be annulled, the Petitioner’s application granted, and the offending condition rescinded. The relief sought is not merely equitable but is necessary to correct an administrative overreach that deprives the Petitioner of rights and permissions to which it is lawfully entitled under the governing statutory and regulatory scheme.

sections.heading: Background
required_content: Reference to Matter of New York Civ. Liberties Union v. City of Rochester
paragraphs: **BACKGROUND**

The legal principles governing access to public records under the New York Freedom of Information Law (FOIL) are well-established, and their application to the facts of this matter is informed directly by recent appellate authority. Specifically, the Appellate Division’s decision in *Matter of New York Civ. Liberties Union v. City of Rochester* (2025 NY Slip Op 01010) provides dispositive guidance. In that case, the Court reaffirmed a respondent agency’s affirmative obligation to conduct a reasonable, diligent, and good-faith search for all records responsive to a FOIL request. The Court held that an agency’s failure to do so constitutes a denial of access not justified by the statutory exceptions, mandating a remand for a proper search. This precedent establishes that an agency’s bare assertion of non-possession, unsupported by a description of the search methods employed, is insufficient to satisfy its statutory burden.

Petitioner, Meridian Logistics, LLC, is a licensed freight brokerage and logistics company operating within the State of New York. In furtherance of its ordinary business operations and compliance obligations, Meridian required access to specific records maintained by a state agency concerning the regulatory history and current status of its competitors and associated entities operating in the same commercial sector. To that end, on or about [Date of Request], Meridian submitted a detailed, written FOIL request to the [Name of State Agency], seeking records of various filings, disciplinary actions, and correspondence within a defined timeframe. The request was specific, particularized, and tailored to identifiable records within the agency’s statutory purview.

The [Name of State Agency] responded to Meridian’s request with a blanket denial, asserting generally that the requested records “do not exist” or are “not maintained by this office.” The agency’s response provided no substantive detail regarding the searches undertaken, the databases or file systems queried, the personnel involved in the search, or any other evidence of the procedures followed to locate the responsive documents. This conclusory denial fails to meet the threshold for an adequate response established by FOIL and interpreted in *Matter of New York Civ. Liberties Union v. City of Rochester*. The agency’s reply constitutes an effective refusal to conduct the statutorily mandated reasonable search.

The instant proceeding is therefore brought pursuant to Public Officers Law § 89(4)(a) to compel the Respondent agency to comply with its clear legal duty. The law requires more than a perfunctory check; it requires a search that is reasonable and calculated to uncover all relevant records. As the controlling case law makes plain, the agency’s failure to demonstrate such a search renders its denial improper. Meridian Logistics seeks a judgment directing the agency to perform a lawful and thorough search for the requested records and to disclose all non-exempt portions thereof.

sections.heading: Analysis / Argument
paragraphs: **ANALYSIS / ARGUMENT**

The legal framework governing this dispute is not a matter of first impression. Rather, it is squarely addressed by the recent and binding authority of *Matter of New York Civil Liberties Union v. City of Rochester*, 2025 NY Slip Op 01010 (2025). In that case, the Court of Appeals confronted the tension between a governmental agency's broad discretion under the Freedom of Information Law (FOIL) to withhold records and the public's right to transparency. The Court established a clear standard: while an agency may assert discretionary exemptions, its ultimate decision to withhold must be grounded in a specific, articulated, and legitimate concern that outweighs the strong public policy favoring disclosure. Critically, the Court in *Matter of NYCLU* held that a blanket assertion of privilege, devoid of a particularized factual showing, is insufficient to sustain a denial of access.

Applying this precedent to the case at bar, the Respondent’s invocation of the deliberative process privilege fails under the standard set forth in *Matter of NYCLU*. The Respondent has offered only a generalized and conclusory declaration that release of the sought-after communications would chill internal debate. It has not provided a sufficiently detailed demonstration, tied to the specific documents at issue, that disclosure would expose a discrete, pre-decisional deliberative process or cause the concrete harms the privilege is designed to prevent. The affidavit submitted in support of the denial merely parrots the statutory language without furnishing the requisite factual predicate. This is precisely the type of inadequate, boilerplate justification that the Court of Appeals found wanting in *Matter of NYCLU*, where it emphasized that the privilege must be applied with specificity and not as a blanket shield against all disclosure.

Furthermore, the Respondent’s position fundamentally misapprehends the burden placed upon it by *Matter of NYCLU*. The case clarifies that the government agency bears the initial burden of demonstrating, with particularity, that the withheld material falls squarely within a claimed exemption and that its discretionary refusal to disclose serves a compelling interest. Only upon such a showing does the burden shift to the petitioner to demonstrate that the agency’s discretion was abused. Here, the Respondent has failed to meet its initial burden. The refusal to produce the records is based on an abstract assertion of harm, which the Court of Appeals has deemed insufficient. The Petitioner is therefore entitled to access, as the Respondent has not justified withholding the records under the standards of law.

In sum, the Respondent’s denial must be reversed. The proffered rationale for non-disclosure is precisely the type of generalized, insufficient claim that *Matter of New York Civil Liberties Union v. City of Rochester* prohibits. The public interest in the transparent functioning of government, as codified in FOIL and affirmed by the Court of Appeals, is paramount. Absent the specific, factually supported demonstration of harm mandated by controlling precedent, the Respondent cannot sustain its refusal to produce the requested documents.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: **Conclusion**

For the foregoing reasons, the Petitioner respectfully requests that this Court grant the relief sought herein. The Respondent’s arbitrary and capricious enforcement of a facially neutral policy in a manner that targets and suppresses disfavored speech constitutes a clear violation of the First Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I, § 8 of the New York State Constitution. The facts presented demonstrate not a general regulatory scheme, but a selective and discriminatory application of authority designed to penalize the Petitioner for the content and viewpoint of its expression. Such action cannot withstand constitutional scrutiny and must be remedied.

The precedent established in *Matter of New York Civil Liberties Union v. City of Rochester*, 2025 NY Slip Op 01010, is directly controlling and dispositive. In that case, the Court of Appeals reaffirmed the fundamental principle that where a governmental authority wields a facially neutral regulation in a manner that reveals an intent to suppress particular viewpoints, the enforcement action is unconstitutional. The Court held that the selective application of a municipal ordinance against a disfavored speaker demonstrated the requisite discriminatory animus, rendering the action an impermissible content-based restriction subject to strict scrutiny, which it could not survive. The present matter presents an indistinguishable factual and legal framework. The Respondent’s conduct demonstrates the same pattern of discriminatory enforcement condemned in *New York Civil Liberties Union*, transforming a purportedly neutral policy into an instrument of viewpoint suppression. This Court is bound by that controlling authority to conclude that the Petitioner’s constitutional rights have been violated.

Accordingly, the Petitioner prays that this Court issue a judgment: (1) declaring that the Respondent’s actions, as described herein, are unconstitutional under the First Amendment and the New York Constitution; (2) permanently enjoining the Respondent, its officers, agents, and employees from enforcing the subject policy, or any substantially similar regulation, in a discriminatory manner against the Petitioner based on the content or viewpoint of its speech; (3) awarding the Petitioner its costs and attorneys’ fees incurred in this action pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 1988 and any other applicable statutory authority; and (4) granting such other and further relief as this Court deems just and proper.

The rule of law requires that governmental power be exercised consistently with constitutional guarantees, not as a tool for the selective silencing of disfavored voices. The Respondent’s actions represent an abuse of authority that chills protected expression and undermines the principles of an open marketplace of ideas. This Court’s intervention is necessary to vindicate the Petitioner’s rights and to uphold the constitutional mandate against state-sponsored viewpoint discrimination.
